slot.brief: Given the expression for electric/gravitational field at a distance, check its dimensional consistency and deduce the correct option by dimensional analysis.

stem: The gravitational field intensity at a distance $r$ from a source is given by $E = \dfrac{A r}{(r^2 + B)^{3/2}}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants. The dimensional formula of $A$ is:

verdicts.working: [E] = LT⁻² (field = acceleration). Since B adds to r², [B] = L², so denominator has dimension L³. Then [A] = [E]·L³/[r] = LT⁻²·L³/L = M⁰L³T⁻².

working:
According to the principle of homogeneity, terms added together must have the same dimensions. Since $B$ is added to $r^2$ in the denominator: $[B] = [r^2] = [\text{L}^2]$. Therefore, the denominator has dimensions: $[(r^2 + B)^{3/2}] = ([\text{L}^2])^{3/2} = [\text{L}^3]$. Gravitational field intensity $E$ is force per unit mass: $[E] = \dfrac{[\text{Force}]}{[\text{Mass}]} = \dfrac{[\text{M}\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}]}{[\text{M}]} = [\text{M}^0\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}]$. From the given equation: $[E] = \dfrac{[A][r]}{[(r^2 + B)^{3/2}]} \implies [\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}] = \dfrac{[A][\text{L}]}{[\text{L}^3]} = \dfrac{[A]}{[\text{L}^2]}$. Solving for $[A]$ gives: $[A] = [\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}][\text{L}^2] = [\text{M}^0\text{L}^3\text{T}^{-2}]$.

Independent check: [E] = LT⁻² (field = acceleration). Since B adds to r², [B] = L², so denominator has dimension L³. Then [A] = [E]·L³/[r] = LT⁻²·L³/L = M⁰L³T⁻².

draft.distractor_notes: A: Forgets the power of 3/2 and treats the denominator as having dimension [L^2], yielding [M^0 L^2 T^-2]. C: Confuses gravitational field intensity with gravitational force ([M L T^-2]), introducing an extra factor of mass to give [M L^3 T^-2]. D: Assumes constant A is identical to the universal gravitational constant G, forgetting the mass factor (since A = GM), which yields [M^-1 L^3 T^-2].
